title: The Chalcedonian Definition
subtitle: The full text of the Definition of Chalcedon (AD 451): one Christ in two natures, without confusion or division, with notes on Nestorius and Eutyches.
intro:
By the middle of the fifth century the church had settled that Christ is fully God. The new fight was over how God and man meet in him. Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, spoke of Christ in ways that seemed to split him into two persons loosely joined, and refused to call Mary Theotokos, God-bearer, as if the one she carried were someone other than God the Son. A monk named Eutyches overcorrected in the opposite direction: the human nature, he taught, was swallowed by the divine like a drop of honey in the sea. One error pulled Christ apart. The other dissolved him.

In October 451, more than five hundred bishops met at Chalcedon, across the water from Constantinople, and drew the line that still holds: one and the same Son, truly God and truly man, made known in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Four adverbs, all negative. The Definition does not explain the mystery of the incarnation. It fences it, naming the four ways the church had learned, at cost, that it breaks.

It is worth being honest about the aftermath. Chalcedon did not produce peace. Whole churches (the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syrian, and Armenian communions) never accepted it, and the wound is fifteen centuries old. But the Definition remains the grammar of every sermon that dares to say God wept, God hungered, God died and rose. Whoever says those sentences is speaking Chalcedon, whether they know the name or not. The bishops gave us permission to say them without blasphemy. That was the point.
text:
Following, then, the holy fathers, we all with one voice teach that it is to be confessed that our Lord Jesus Christ is one and the same Son, the same perfect in Godhead and the same perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man, the same of a reasonable soul and body; consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead, and the same consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin; begotten of the Father before the ages according to the Godhead, and in these last days, for us and for our salvation, born of the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, according to the manhood.

One and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-begotten, made known in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the distinction of natures being in no way taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person and one Subsistence, not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, and Only-begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ.

As the prophets from the beginning have declared concerning him, and the Lord Jesus Christ himself hath taught us, and the Creed of the holy fathers hath handed down to us.

annotations.note: The Definition presents itself as conservation, not invention. The bishops claimed to be adding nothing to Nicaea and Constantinople, only stating what the church had always confessed, against new ways of losing it.

The two truths the whole document exists to hold together. Every christological heresy is a way of quietly deleting one of these words, and most modern errors about Jesus are still one of these two deletions wearing new clothes.

annotations.phrase: consubstantial with us according to the manhood
annotations.note: The same word Nicaea used of Christ and the Father, homoousios, is here used of Christ and us. He is as fully human as he is fully divine. His solidarity with us is not a costume. It is shared nature.

annotations.phrase: in all things like unto us, without sin
annotations.note: An echo of Hebrews 4:15. Sinlessness is the only exception, and it is not an exception to humanity. Sin is a corruption of human nature, not an ingredient of it. He is more human than we are, not less.

Greek for 'God-bearer.' Nestorius would allow only 'Christ-bearer,' as if Mary's child were not God the Son. The council kept the harder word, not to exalt Mary, but to protect the identity of her son. The one born of her is the eternal Word.

The first two adverbs, aimed at Eutyches. The natures are not blended into a hybrid, and the deity does not mutate into flesh. God remains God, man remains man, in one Person. The union does not destroy what it unites.

The second pair, aimed at Nestorianism. There are not two sons, a divine one and a human one taking turns. Everything Jesus does, the one Person does. The infant in the manger and the Word upholding the universe are the same 'he.'

annotations.phrase: the property of each nature being preserved
annotations.note: The divine nature keeps everything divine. The human nature keeps everything human: hunger, sleep, tears, death. This line is why a preacher may say 'God died for you' without claiming deity perished: the one Person died, in his human nature.

The technical center: one hypostasis. The natures answer 'what is he?' God and man. The Person answers 'who is he?' The Son, singular. Two whats, one who. It is the most useful sentence of theology most Christians have never been taught.
